content: Efforts by stakeholders are essential to adopt and adapt the guidelines and to develop implementation plans that are specifically tailored to the local context and the unique needs of each country’s health system. These efforts must consider the preliminary work conducted through stakeholder surveys. The WHO Secretariat will continue to collaborate with all stakeholders and implementers to identify barriers and facilitators to the successful implementation of the guidelines. Achieving consistent and effective rounds of mass drug administration (MDA) for lymphatic filariasis (LF) using the alternative regimens recommended in this guideline will require the integration of these new regimens into national guidelines for LF and neglected tropical diseases. This will also necessitate strong coordination and advanced planning of MDA activities in alignment with national health system implementation agendas. To support countries in their implementation efforts, the WHO will provide a field guide for program managers. This guide will include planning and implementation tools for use at both national and subnational levels in endemic countries. It will feature dedicated sections on leadership, advocacy, communication, staffing, human resources, medicine supplies, supply chain management, system organization, strategic planning, community-level implementation, and financial implications. In accordance with existing WHO guidance on LF, this guideline aligns with the Global Programme to Eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis (GPELF) strategic framework. This framework is based on a public health approach aimed at eliminating LF as a public health problem. The approach ensures that consistent and effective rounds of MDA are delivered at the population level to interrupt LF transmission within communities. Implementation strategies are based on simplified and standardized approaches that have been proven technically feasible on a large scale, even in resource-limited health systems. These strategies consider factors such as health system organization and capacity, human resources, medicine availability, financial resources, feasibility, and community-level acceptability. The implementation of this guideline as part of the GPELF framework will assist countries in addressing the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by 2030. Specifically, it will contribute to poverty reduction (SDG 1), health (SDG 3), quality education (SDG 4), gender equality (SDG 5), good jobs and economic growth (SDG 8), and reduced inequalities (SDG 10). WHO will monitor the impact of the guideline’s implementation by collecting data on the number of countries and implementation units (IUs) that adopt alternative LF MDA regimens in line with WHO recommendations. The impact will be evaluated by assessing progress toward meeting LF elimination criteria, such as the interruption of transmission while using the alternative regimens. Progress at the IU and country levels will be routinely monitored by WHO regional offices and discussed within Regional Programme Review Groups. Epidemiological data will be closely reviewed on an ongoing basis. Data will be collected through each country’s annual reporting to WHO via the Joint Application Package, as well as through documentation in Regional Programme Review Group meeting reports and country validation dossiers for elimination. Annual data from LF-endemic countries will be stored in the WHO preventive chemotherapy databank, and global progress updates on LF elimination will be shared in the WHO Weekly Epidemiological Record. The WHO Department of Control of Neglected Tropical Diseases will use reported data to monitor the coverage of current and alternative MDA regimens. Key indicators will include geographical coverage (the proportion of LF-endemic IUs that have initiated MDA), epidemiological coverage (the proportion of the total population that ingested the medicines during MDA), and effective coverage (the proportion of IUs implementing MDA that directly observed at least 65% of the population ingesting the medicines). These data will also be used to assess the impact of MDA regimens by evaluating the proportion of IUs meeting elimination targets, such as sentinel and spot-check surveys meeting epidemiological success criteria (<1% microfilaraemia or <2% antigenaemia) and the proportion of IUs passing Transmission Assessment Surveys (TAS). The WHO International Drug Monitoring Programme will continue to monitor and evaluate individual case safety reports submitted by Member States regarding the administration of ivermectin, diethylcarbamazine, and/or albendazole. These data will be stored in the WHO VigiBase and made accessible through VigiAccess™. Monitoring reports will be generated and reviewed annually through interdepartmental collaboration between the WHO Department of Control of Neglected Tropical Diseases and the WHO Department of Essential Medicines and Health Products. To assist countries in comprehensive monitoring and evaluation efforts during and after implementation, the WHO field guide for program managers will provide detailed guidance on epidemiological monitoring, adverse event monitoring, and the integration of national pharmacovigilance systems with MDA activities. Research trials are ongoing to generate additional evidence on the efficacy and safety of current and new MDA regimens for LF. As new evidence becomes available, amendments to this guideline may be issued in accordance with the WHO handbook on guideline development. The WHO Department of Control of Neglected Tropical Diseases will review new evidence two years after the guideline’s release and reassess the need for updates. The guideline development group will remain focused on ensuring effective, safe, and accelerated strategies to enable countries to interrupt LF transmission and achieve elimination of the disease as a public health problem.
